scenes.headline: How a vector index drops its vectors
scenes.sub: LEANN keeps the graph and recomputes the rest
scenes.say: Hi, I'm Sloe! Today: how a vector index can throw away its vectors and still find the nearest neighbours.

scenes.text: A graph search visits only a few thousand nodes. So store the graph, and compute the vector for a node only when a query reaches it.
scenes.mark: compute the vector for a node only when a query reaches it
scenes.say: A search visits only a few thousand nodes. So keep the graph, and make each vector only when a query arrives.

steps.say: The query walks the graph, which holds only lists of neighbour ids.
Each step lands on a node whose distance it needs.
The node's text is fetched and sent through the embedding model.
The fresh distances steer the walk, and the best ten come back.

left.title: Standard HNSW
items: A padded neighbour list per node
left.say: A standard index keeps every vector and a padded neighbour list per node.

right.title: LEANN
right.say: LEANN keeps only a compact neighbour list. The vector is gone.

scenes.label: smaller index file, on 20,000 chunks
scenes.say: On twenty thousand chunks the index file shrank by about ninety-one percent.

scenes.title: Chunks embedded per query
scenes.note: every one is a model forward pass
scenes.say: The cost moves to query time. Each query embeds hundreds to thousands of chunks, one model pass each.

scenes.text: LEANN trades disk for compute. It fits an archive you search rarely and cannot fit one you search constantly.
scenes.say: LEANN trades disk for compute. Great for an archive you rarely search.

recap: No vectors stored, only the graph
scenes.say: No stored vectors, a much smaller index, and a model call for every node a query visits.
